articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's Short-Term Rental Fight Heads to Tallahassee
articles.dek: County commissioners want local control over vacation rentals. State preemption says no. A new bill could change that—or make things worse.
brief: Escambia County commissioners have joined a coalition of Florida localities pushing for repeal of the 2011 state preemption on short-term rental regulation
A bill advancing through the legislature would restore some local authority but includes provisions critics say favor the vacation rental industry
Residents in Pensacola Beach and unincorporated areas report ongoing conflicts between STR operations and traditional neighborhoods
articles.body:
The house on Ariola Drive looks like every other mid-century beach cottage on Pensacola Beach. Wood siding gone silver from salt air. A carport underneath. The kind of place a family might have owned for three generations.

Except the family sold it in 2019. Now it sleeps 14. The property management company calls it "Sunset Serenity." The neighbors call code enforcement.

"Every weekend it's a different group," said Margaret Collier, who has lived next door for 22 years. "Trash cans overflowing. Cars parked on the grass. I called the county so many times I stopped counting."

Escambia County can cite the property for noise violations. For parking violations. For trash violations. What it cannot do—what no Florida county or municipality can do—is tell the owner he can't rent it out by the night.

That power was stripped away 15 years ago. Now a coalition of local governments wants it back.

The Preemption Problem

In 2011, Florida's legislature passed a law prohibiting local governments from enacting any new regulations on vacation rentals. The statute grandfathered existing ordinances but froze everything else. Counties that had rules before 2011 could keep them. Counties that didn't were locked out.

Escambia County had minimal regulations at the time. Pensacola Beach—which sits on Santa Rosa Island but falls under Escambia County's jurisdiction—had none specifically targeting short-term rentals.

"We were caught flat-footed," said Escambia County Commissioner Steven Barry. "In 2011, vacation rentals weren't the issue they are today. Nobody anticipated what was coming."

What came was Airbnb, VRBO and a half-dozen other platforms that turned home-sharing from a niche activity into a multibillion-dollar industry. In Escambia County, short-term rental listings have increased 340% since 2015, according to data the county compiled from AirDNA, an industry analytics firm.

The preemption law was loosened slightly in 2014 to allow some local oversight—registration requirements, safety inspections, tax collection—but the core prohibition remained. Local governments cannot ban short-term rentals. Cannot cap their numbers. Cannot restrict them to certain zones.

A New Bill, Old Arguments

House Bill 1247, sponsored by Rep. Daniel Perez of Miami, would partially lift the preemption. Under the bill, counties could regulate "density and frequency" of short-term rentals, establish minimum distance requirements between properties, and create overlay districts where additional restrictions apply.

The bill passed its first committee vote 11-4 in March. A Senate companion, SB 1580, is scheduled for its second reading next week.

Escambia County Administrator Wes Moreno testified in support of the bill during the House committee hearing. "Local governments are not asking to ban vacation rentals," he told legislators. "We're asking for tools to address legitimate quality-of-life concerns in residential neighborhoods."

But the bill has drawn opposition from multiple directions.

The Florida Vacation Rental Management Association argues the legislation would create a "patchwork" of regulations that would burden property owners and confuse tourists. In written testimony, the group's lobbyist warned that local restrictions could suppress property values and reduce tourist spending.

On the other side, some housing advocates say the bill doesn't go far enough. Anna Chen, policy director for the Florida Housing Coalition, said density caps alone won't address the fundamental problem: vacation rentals converting long-term housing stock into tourist accommodations.

"You can limit how many STRs are on a block, but you're still losing units from the rental market," Chen said. "In a place like Pensacola Beach, where housing is already constrained, that has real consequences."

The Local Divide

Not everyone in Escambia County wants more regulation.

Rick Patterson owns three rental properties in the Pensacola Beach area. All three are registered with the county and listed on VRBO. He pays the required tourist development taxes. He screens renters. He responds to complaints.

"I'm a good actor," Patterson said. "My neighbors know how to reach me. But now I'm going to get lumped in with the bad apples because the county couldn't figure out enforcement."

Patterson said he supports reasonable rules—maximum occupancy limits, noise ordinances, parking requirements—but opposes density caps that could effectively grandfather existing rentals while blocking new ones.

"That's just pulling up the ladder," he said.

The Santa Rosa Island Authority, the special district that manages Pensacola Beach's leaseholds, has taken no official position on HB 1247. Board chair Karen Sindel said members are divided.

"Some leaseholders want us to push hard for local control," Sindel said. "Others are rental owners themselves. We're trying to gather input before we weigh in."

Waiting for Tallahassee

Escambia County commissioners voted unanimously in February to send a resolution to Tallahassee supporting "restoration of local authority over short-term rental regulation." Similar resolutions have passed in Santa Rosa County, Walton County and more than 30 other Florida jurisdictions.

Whether that pressure moves the legislature remains uncertain. The bill's sponsor, Perez, has significant campaign contributions from real estate interests, though he has framed the legislation as a compromise between local control and property rights.

For residents like Collier, the policy debate feels abstract compared to the Friday night noise next door.

"I don't care who regulates it," she said. "I just want someone to."

HB 1247 faces two more committee stops before reaching the House floor. The legislative session ends May 30.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The $47 Million Hole on Palafox
articles.dek: Three years after demolition, the former Sears site downtown sits empty. The developers blame permits. The city blames the developers. Neighbors just want answers.
brief: The former Sears site at 657 N. Palafox has sat vacant since demolition in early 2023, with no construction activity despite a $47 million mixed-use project approval.
Developer Palafox Gateway LLC and City of Pensacola officials trade blame over permit delays and infrastructure requirements.
Downtown business owners and residents say the vacant lot has become a dumping ground and safety concern.
articles.body:
The chain-link fence went up three years ago. It's still there.

At 657 N. Palafox Street, where a Sears department store stood for six decades, there is now a hole. Not a construction site. Not a foundation. A hole—roughly 1.2 acres of packed dirt, scattered concrete rubble, and whatever people throw over the fence when they think nobody's watching.

On a Tuesday afternoon in late April, a shopping cart sat upside down near the southwest corner. A mattress leaned against what remained of a retaining wall. Three pigeons picked at something in the center of the lot.

"I've stopped asking when something's going to happen," said Marcus Trahan, who owns Trahan's Barbershop two blocks south. "I just assume this is what it is now."

The Promise

In February 2022, Pensacola City Council approved a development agreement with Palafox Gateway LLC for a $47 million mixed-use project on the site. The plans showed an eight-story building with 156 residential units, 12,000 square feet of ground-floor retail, and a 280-space parking garage. Renderings depicted young professionals walking dogs past outdoor café seating. The project was called "The Beacon."

Then-Mayor Grover Robinson called it "transformational." Council President Jared Moore said it would "anchor the north end of Palafox for the next fifty years."

Demolition of the Sears building began in October 2022 and finished in January 2023. Since then, nothing.

The Blame

Ask the city why construction hasn't started, and officials point to Palafox Gateway.

"The developer has not submitted complete permit applications for vertical construction," said David Forte, Pensacola's director of development services, in an email response to questions. "We cannot issue permits for applications we don't have."

Forte said the city received a grading permit application in March 2023, which was approved. A foundation permit application came in August 2023 but was rejected for incomplete structural engineering documentation. A revised application was submitted in February 2024, then withdrawn by the developer in June 2024.

"Since June 2024, we have received no permit applications related to this project," Forte wrote.

Ask Palafox Gateway, and the story sounds different.

Robert Mallin, managing partner of the development group, said in a phone interview that the city's infrastructure requirements have made the project financially unworkable as originally designed.

"When we signed the development agreement, we were told the existing water and sewer infrastructure could handle the project," Mallin said. "Eighteen months later, they came back and said we needed to fund $3.2 million in utility upgrades. That wasn't in our pro forma."

Mallin said the company has been trying to renegotiate the development agreement since late 2024 but has not received a formal response from the city.

Forte disputed this characterization. "Infrastructure requirements are clearly outlined in our development review process and would have been communicated during pre-application meetings," he wrote. He declined to comment on specific negotiations, citing ongoing discussions.

The Waiting

Rhonda Sasser has lived in the Aragon apartment building, one block east of the site, for eleven years. She remembers when the Sears was open—"not busy, but open"—and remembers the excitement when the development was announced.

"They had this big presentation at the community center," Sasser said, sitting on a bench outside her building. "Showed us all these pictures. Said it would bring new restaurants, new shops. That was four years ago."

She said the vacant lot has attracted problems. She's called the city about illegal dumping at least a dozen times. Twice she's seen people sleeping on the property. Once, in the summer of 2024, someone started a fire that burned for two hours before firefighters arrived.

"It's not a construction site. It's an eyesore," Sasser said. "And nobody will tell us what's happening."

The Pensacola Downtown Improvement Board, which manages the Community Redevelopment Area that includes the site, has limited authority over private property. Executive Director Curt Morse said the board has reached out to Palafox Gateway multiple times but has not received substantive updates.

"We can encourage. We can't compel," Morse said. "Our hope is that they either move forward or sell to someone who will."

The Money

The 2022 development agreement included $4.8 million in public incentives: a $2.1 million infrastructure grant, $1.6 million in tax increment financing, and a $1.1 million brownfield cleanup grant from the Florida Department of Environmental Protection.

According to city records, only the brownfield grant has been fully disbursed. The infrastructure grant has paid out $340,000 for demolition-related work. The TIF funds, which are distributed based on increased property tax revenue from the completed project, have not been triggered because there is no completed project.

The development agreement includes a clause requiring construction to begin within 24 months of demolition completion. That deadline passed in January 2025. The agreement also includes a provision allowing the city to terminate for cause if the developer fails to meet milestones.

Asked whether the city is considering termination, Forte wrote: "The city is evaluating all options and has been in communication with the developer's representatives."

Mallin said termination would be "counterproductive."

"We've invested $6 million in this project already," he said. "We're not walking away. We just need a path forward that makes financial sense."

The Alternatives

In the meantime, the lot sits.

At least two other developers have expressed interest in the site, according to commercial real estate broker Ellen Wexler of Studer Properties. She said she's received inquiries but cannot discuss specifics because Palafox Gateway has not listed the property for sale.

"It's a prime location," Wexler said. "North Palafox is undervalued. Whoever builds there will do well. The question is when."

Some neighbors have suggested interim uses—a temporary park, a farmer's market, public parking. City officials said such uses would require cooperation from the property owner.

Council member Jennifer Brahier, whose District 6 includes the site, said she's frustrated but hesitant to interfere with a private development.

"I'm not in the business of telling property owners what to do with their land," Brahier said. "But I am in the business of representing the people who live around it. And they deserve better than this."

She said she plans to request a formal update from city staff at the May council meeting.

The View

On a Friday evening in early May, the sun dropped behind the tree line west of downtown. The hole on Palafox caught the last light, its dirt surface turning briefly orange before fading to gray.

Marcus Trahan was locking up his barbershop. He glanced north at the fence.

"You know what I think about when I look at that?" he said. "I think about all the times I've heard 'downtown is coming back.' All the money they've spent on the baseball stadium, the new waterfront stuff. And then there's this."

He shook his head.

"Maybe it's coming back," he said. "But it ain't there yet."

articles.label: Local News
articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Brings 300,000 Visitors—and a Strain on Everything Else
articles.dek: Hotels are full, restaurants are slammed, and traffic on the Three Mile Bridge backs up to Cervantes. Inside the annual economic boom that tests Pensacola's limits.
brief: An estimated 300,000 visitors descended on Pensacola for Blue Angels Homecoming Week, filling every hotel room within 30 miles of NAS Pensacola
Local restaurants reported wait times exceeding two hours while traffic on the Pensacola Bay Bridge created backups stretching into downtown
Visit Pensacola estimates the four-day event generated $45 million in direct economic impact for Escambia and Santa Rosa counties
articles.body:
At 11:47 a.m. on Saturday, Maria Gonzalez stood behind the host stand at The Grand Marlin on Pensacola Beach and watched the wait time on her tablet climb past 135 minutes. The restaurant had been on a two-hour wait since 10:30. She'd stopped apologizing.

"People understand," Gonzalez said. "It's Homecoming. Everyone knows what they're getting into."

What they were getting into was the annual stress test that Blue Angels Homecoming Week puts on every piece of infrastructure Pensacola has. The roads. The restaurants. The hotel rooms. The septic systems on Pensacola Beach. For four days in early May, the region absorbs a population surge that would overwhelm most cities this size—and somehow keeps functioning.

This year's edition drew an estimated 300,000 visitors across the weekend, according to preliminary figures from Visit Pensacola. That's roughly the equivalent of adding the entire population of Escambia County to an area designed to handle a fraction of that load.

The Bridge Problem

By 8 a.m. Friday, traffic on the Three Mile Bridge had slowed to a crawl. By 9:30, it wasn't moving at all. The backup extended past Cervantes Street, more than two miles from the bridge's western approach.

Pensacola Police Department spokesperson Sgt. David Williams said officers were deployed to 14 intersections along the route to NAS Pensacola, where the air show takes place. The Florida Highway Patrol added six troopers to manage beach-bound traffic on the Bob Sikes Bridge connecting Gulf Breeze to Pensacola Beach.

"We plan for this all year," Williams said. "But you can only move so many cars across a two-lane bridge."

The bottleneck is structural and familiar. The Three Mile Bridge, which connects Pensacola to Gulf Breeze across Pensacola Bay, was designed for daily commuter traffic—not 75,000 people trying to reach the same destination within a three-hour window. Widening it would require years of construction and hundreds of millions of dollars. So every May, the region improvises.

Some locals have learned to game the system. They arrive at NAS Pensacola before 7 a.m. or watch from boats anchored in the bay. Others simply leave town for the weekend.

"I love the Blue Angels," said Tom Hutchinson, a 34-year Gulf Breeze resident. "But I've seen them a hundred times. I don't need to sit in traffic for three hours to see them again."

$45 Million in Four Days

The economic math makes the headaches worthwhile—at least from a regional perspective.

Visit Pensacola's preliminary analysis estimates the 2026 Homecoming generated $45 million in direct economic impact across Escambia and Santa Rosa counties. That figure includes hotel revenue, restaurant spending, gas purchases and retail sales. It does not account for secondary effects like tips to service workers or long-term tourism conversion.

"This is our Super Bowl," said Visit Pensacola President and CEO Darien Schaefer. "Nothing else we do comes close to this kind of concentrated impact."

Hotel occupancy across the two-county region hit 98.7% on Friday and Saturday nights, according to data from STR, a hospitality analytics firm. Average daily rates spiked to $289—nearly double the typical May weekend rate of $152.

The compression forced visitors into creative arrangements. Vacation rentals on Perdido Key, normally a 45-minute drive from NAS Pensacola, reported full bookings. RV parks in Cantonment sold out. One family from Birmingham told The Flightline they were staying in Mobile and driving in each day—a 120-mile round trip—because it was the closest available lodging they could find when they booked in March.

The Restaurant Crunch

At Fish House on Pensacola's waterfront, general manager Chris Bates said the restaurant served 1,847 covers on Saturday alone. A typical busy Saturday in May might see 900.

"We brought in extra staff from our other properties," Bates said. "We ran two full kitchen crews. And we still had tickets backing up."

The strain rippled across the region's hospitality sector. Line cooks worked double shifts. Servers reported earning more in tips over the four-day stretch than they typically make in two weeks. Dishwashers became the most valuable employees in the building.

Not every establishment chose to participate. McGuire's Irish Pub, one of Pensacola's most popular destinations, stuck with its normal staffing levels and accepted the chaos.

"We're not going to turn ourselves inside out for one weekend," said a McGuire's manager who declined to give her name because she wasn't authorized to speak publicly. "The regulars still need somewhere to eat. We take care of them first."

The Infrastructure Nobody Sees

The visible strain—traffic, crowds, wait times—obscures the invisible systems working at capacity.

Emerald Coast Utilities Authority reported water usage on Pensacola Beach spiked 340% above normal Saturday levels. The island's wastewater treatment capacity, designed for a residential population of roughly 4,000, processed flows consistent with a temporary population exceeding 35,000.

"We add portable facilities and we stage vacuum trucks," said ECUA spokesperson Nathalie Bowers. "But the permanent infrastructure can only do so much. We're always operating at the edge during Homecoming."

Pensacola Beach's limited road network creates additional complications. Santa Rosa Island has essentially one main road—Via de Luna—running its length. When traffic stops, there's no alternate route. Emergency vehicles have to thread through gridlock.

Escambia County Emergency Medical Services staged two additional ambulances on the beach for the weekend and positioned a supervisor vehicle near the entrance to the Bob Sikes Bridge to coordinate response.

"We didn't have any major incidents this year," said EMS Chief David Matthews. "But we plan for them."

The Show Itself

All of this exists to support a 45-minute performance.

The Blue Angels, the Navy's flight demonstration squadron, have called NAS Pensacola home since 1954. Homecoming marks the team's first local performance of each season—a point of civic pride that transcends the economic calculations.

Saturday's show drew an estimated crowd of 125,000 to the base, according to Navy officials. They spread across the flight line, sat on coolers and lawn chairs, and craned their necks as six F/A-18 Super Hornets carved trails across a cloudless sky.

"This never gets old," said Angela Morrison, who grew up in Pensacola and now lives in Atlanta. She makes the trip back every year with her two children. "I want them to understand where they come from. And this is part of it."

The 2026 team, led by Commanding Officer Cmdr. Alex Armitage, performed the full demonstration routine, including the signature Diamond 360 and the Opposing Knife Edge pass. The crowd erupted at each maneuver. Car alarms triggered by the sonic pressure added to the din.

The Morning After

By Sunday evening, the exodus had begun. The Three Mile Bridge backed up again—this time heading west, as visitors funneled toward I-10 and points beyond.

On Pensacola Beach, crews from Escambia County Public Works fanned out to collect trash left on the sand. Restaurant staff deep-cleaned kitchens that had run nonstop for 72 hours. Hotel housekeepers stripped rooms and reset for the next wave of guests.

Monday morning, the rhythm returned to something like normal. Traffic flowed. Wait times dropped. The portable toilets disappeared from the beach.

In 362 days, it will all happen again.

Visit Pensacola's Schaefer acknowledged the strain the event places on the region but argued the benefits justify the disruption.

"This is who we are," he said. "We're a Navy town. We're a Blue Angels town. One weekend of inconvenience is a small price for what this means to the community."

Maria Gonzalez, back at her host stand at The Grand Marlin on Monday, disagreed only slightly.

"It's worth it," she said. "But ask me again on Saturday and I might give you a different answer."
